response.title: How much battery and solar do I need to run an air conditioner in a camper van during the day in Florida heat?
response.answer:
To run an air conditioner in a camper van during the day in Florida summer heat, I would recommend 800–1,200 watts of solar and a 10–15 kWh lithium battery bank if you want reliable cooling for 8–10 hours without running a generator.

However, there's a catch: a typical camper van roof cannot fit enough solar panels to continuously power an air conditioner in Florida heat. You'll likely need a combination of rooftop solar, battery storage, and possibly alternator charging.

1. How much electricity does the AC need?

The biggest factor is which air conditioner you use.

These are planning ranges, not fixed consumption figures. A variable-speed AC can use less power once the van cools down, while direct sunlight, poor insulation, and frequent door openings increase consumption.

For Florida, I would design around an efficient AC averaging 700–900 watts during the hottest part of the day, especially if the van is parked in full sun.

markup:
To run an air conditioner in a camper van during the day in Florida summer heat, I would recommend **800–1,200 watts of solar and a 10–15 kWh lithium battery bank** if you want reliable cooling for 8–10 hours without running a generator.

However, there's a catch: **a typical camper van roof cannot fit enough solar panels to continuously power an air conditioner in Florida heat.** You'll likely need a combination of rooftop solar, battery storage, and possibly alternator charging.

## 1. How much electricity does the AC need?

The biggest factor is which air conditioner you use.

| AC type | Typical running power | Energy for 8 hours |
|---|---:|---:|
| Efficient 12V/48V DC van AC | 400–700 W | 3.2–5.6 kWh |
| Efficient inverter rooftop AC | 600–1,000 W | 4.8–8 kWh |
| Conventional rooftop RV AC | 1,200–1,800 W | 9.6–14.4 kWh |

These are planning ranges, not fixed consumption figures. A variable-speed AC can use less power once the van cools down, while direct sunlight, poor insulation, and frequent door openings increase consumption.

For Florida, I would design around an efficient AC averaging **700–900 watts during the hottest part of the day**, especially if the van is parked in full sun.

## 2. How much solar and battery do you actually need?

Here are three practical configurations for an 8-hour daytime cooling target.

<box gap={3}>
  <row align="center" gap={3}>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      <text weight="medium">Small system</text>
      <title size="lg">600 W solar + 5 kWh battery</title>
      <text color="secondary" size="sm">Suitable for an exceptionally efficient DC AC, moderate cooling demands, and good sunshine. Limited reserve.</text>
    </box>
    <badge color="warning">Marginal</badge>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="center" gap={3}>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      <text weight="medium">Balanced system</text>
      <title size="lg">1,000 W solar + 10 kWh battery</title>
      <text color="secondary" size="sm">A reasonable target for efficient AC and 8–10 hours of daytime cooling, with some reserve for clouds.</text>
    </box>
    <badge color="success">Recommended</badge>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="center" gap={3}>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      <text weight="medium">High-capacity system</text>
      <title size="lg">1,200–1,600 W solar + 15 kWh battery</title>
      <text color="secondary" size="sm">More reserve for extended cooling, higher AC consumption, and variable weather. Often requires deployable panels.</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

The larger battery doesn't create energy: it must still be recharged. For repeated days without driving or plugging in, solar production must cover the daily AC load.

## 3. What does solar actually produce in Florida?

Florida has a good solar resource, but summer afternoon thunderstorms, clouds, panel heat, and flat roof mounting reduce actual output. Solar resource estimates for Florida average around 5–6 peak-sun-hours annually, depending on location. <Cite ref="turn374742search3"/>

For conservative planning, I'll use **4 effective peak-sun-hours and 80% system efficiency**.

| Solar array | Estimated daily production |
|---|---:|
| 400 W | 1.3 kWh |
| 600 W | 1.9 kWh |
| 800 W | 2.6 kWh |
| 1,000 W | 3.2 kWh |
| 1,200 W | 3.8 kWh |
| 1,600 W | 5.1 kWh |

Compare that with an AC consuming 800 W for 8 hours: **6.4 kWh per day**.

Even 1,000 W of solar would only replace approximately half that energy under these assumptions.

## 4. Interactive battery and solar calculator

Adjust the AC power and cooling duration to estimate the battery and solar requirements.

{@body const [hours,setHours] = DIL.useState(8)}
{@body const [solar,setSolar] = DIL.useState(800)}
{@body const [sun,setSun] = DIL.useState(4)}
{@body const consumption = watts*hours/1000}
{@body const generation = solar*sun*.8/1000}
{@body const deficit = Math.max(0,consumption-generation)}
{@body const battery = deficit/.8}

    </row>

    </box>
  </box>
</box>

## 5. Choose an efficient AC first

A low-power variable-speed DC unit can significantly reduce the size of the electrical system.

For example, the <Entity category="product" value="Dometic CoolAir RTX 2000" disambig="12V rooftop air conditioner"/> is a DC-powered rooftop cooling unit. Its published specifications include variable current consumption depending on operating mode, so its energy use can vary substantially. <Cite refs={["turn374742search24","turn374742search28"]}/>

<AsyncImageGroup query={["Dometic CoolAir RTX 2000 rooftop camper van air conditioner installed","camper van roof covered with solar panels air conditioner"]} aspectRatio="5:3" shop_eligible={true}/>

Keep in mind that electrical efficiency and cooling capacity are different. A very small, efficient AC may not be powerful enough to hold 72°F inside a sun-exposed van in Florida.

Also prioritize roof and wall insulation, reflective windshield covers, window shading, and a light-colored roof.

text:
To run an air conditioner in a camper van during the day in Florida summer heat, I would recommend 800–1,200 watts of solar and a 10–15 kWh lithium battery bank if you want reliable cooling for 8–10 hours without running a generator.

However, there's a catch: a typical camper van roof cannot fit enough solar panels to continuously power an air conditioner in Florida heat. You'll likely need a combination of rooftop solar, battery storage, and possibly alternator charging.

1. How much electricity does the AC need?

The biggest factor is which air conditioner you use.

Conventional rooftop RV AC

These are planning ranges, not fixed consumption figures. A variable-speed AC can use less power once the van cools down, while direct sunlight, poor insulation, and frequent door openings increase consumption.

For Florida, I would design around an efficient AC averaging 700–900 watts during the hottest part of the day, especially if the van is parked in full sun.

2. How much solar and battery do you actually need?

Here are three practical configurations for an 8-hour daytime cooling target.

Small system

600 W solar + 5 kWh battery

Suitable for an exceptionally efficient DC AC, moderate cooling demands, and good sunshine. Limited reserve.

Marginal

Balanced system

1,000 W solar + 10 kWh battery

A reasonable target for efficient AC and 8–10 hours of daytime cooling, with some reserve for clouds.

Recommended

High-capacity system

1,200–1,600 W solar + 15 kWh battery

More reserve for extended cooling, higher AC consumption, and variable weather. Often requires deployable panels.

The larger battery doesn't create energy: it must still be recharged. For repeated days without driving or plugging in, solar production must cover the daily AC load.

3. What does solar actually produce in Florida?

Florida has a good solar resource, but summer afternoon thunderstorms, clouds, panel heat, and flat roof mounting reduce actual output. Solar resource estimates for Florida average around 5–6 peak-sun-hours annually, depending on location.

Even 1,000 W of solar would only replace approximately half that energy under these assumptions.

5. Choose an efficient AC first

A low-power variable-speed DC unit can significantly reduce the size of the electrical system.

For example, the Dometic CoolAir RTX 2000 is a DC-powered rooftop cooling unit. Its published specifications include variable current consumption depending on operating mode, so its energy use can vary substantially.

Keep in mind that electrical efficiency and cooling capacity are different. A very small, efficient AC may not be powerful enough to hold 72°F inside a sun-exposed van in Florida.

Also prioritize roof and wall insulation, reflective windshield covers, window shading, and a light-colored roof.
